Learning Objectives
Assess shoulder anatomy pertinent to successful shoulder arthroscopy.
Describe an appropriate preoperative clinical evaluation.
Determine appropriate indications and applications for shoulder arthroscopy.
Specify the key components of successful shoulder arthroscopy, including setup, patient
positioning, approach, and diagnostic evaluation.
Shoulder Arthroscopy Technique


Indications
Indications for shoulder arthroscopy are broad and continue to expand. They include
rotator cuff disease,4 shoulder instability,5 labral pathology,6 and biceps tendon
pathology.7 In addition, shoulder arthroscopy can be used for removal of loose or
foreign bodies and for irrigation/débridement and synovectomy of a septic shoulder
joint8,9 (Resources 1 through 3).
Contraindications

Contraindications
Few contraindications exist for shoulder arthroscopy. Although advanced shoulder
arthritis may be considered a contraindication for shoulder arthroscopy, evidence exists
that select patients with glenohumeral arthritis may benefit from an arthroscopic
procedure.10 Certain procedures, such as Latarjet coracoid transfer, can be performed
via an open or arthroscopic approach,11 with approach selection based on surgeon
preference.
Anesthesia and Patient Positioning
The lateral decubitus and beach-chair positions are starting methods for patient positioning
for shoulder arthroscopy.
The lateral decubitus position allows for joint distraction and may limit the risk of cerebral
hypoperfusion.
The beach-chair position allows for adjustment of the position of the surgical extremity and
allows for easy conversion to an open approach if necessary.
General and regional anesthesia may be used for shoulder arthroscopy.


Anesthesia and Patient Positioning
Lateral decubitus and beach-chair positioning are safe and effective methods for
performing shoulder arthroscopy.12,13 (Video 1) The lateral decubitus position allows for
joint distraction, which may make visualization and execution of intra-articular work
more feasible. It also may limit the possibility of cerebral hypoperfusion with
hypotensive anesthesia. The patient is positioned laterally on a padded surgical table
with a bean bag. A strap may be placed around the patient on the torso/pelvis, and all
bony prominences should be well padded. Ensure the peroneal and saphenous nerves
are padded on the bottom and top legs, respectively, and that the down arm is properly
padded. The head is positioned in neutral, and an axillary roll is placed in the
contralateral armpit to support neurovascular structures, with the arm placed on an arm
board. The surgical extremity is assembled with in-line traction of 5 to 15 lbs applied. The
arm is positioned in approximately 20° of forward flexion and 30° to 50° of abduction.
An optional second traction strap may be applied to aid in direct lateral traction of the
shoulder joint. The table may be tilted 20° to 30° posteriorly to position the glenoid
parallel to the floor.14 An aerial depiction of the operating room setup for left shoulder
arthroscopy with the patient in the lateral decubitus position is shown in Figure 1.12 An
intraoperative example of a patient in the lateral decubitus position is shown in Figure 2.

(Image courtesy of Donald J. Scholten II, MD, PhD, Winston-Salem, NC, and Brian R.

Advantages of the beach-chair position include access to adjust surgical arm positioning
to facilitate arthroscopy and the potential to easily transition to an open approach if
necessary. The patient is positioned in a 10° to 15° Trendelenburg position on a table
with an adjustable head rest and movable back and foot sections. The knees are flexed
to 30° to take pressure off the sciatic nerve, and the thorax is brought upright with
approximately 40° to 60° of hip flexion. The cervical spine is maintained in a neutral
position. The nonsurgical arm is placed in a stationary arm holder, and the surgical arm
is prepared and ultimately positioned in an adjustable arm positioner for the procedure.
An aerial depiction of the surgical room setup for left shoulder arthroscopy with the
patient in the beach-chair positioning is shown in Figure 2. The surgical team is
positioned on the surgical side of the patient. An intraoperative example of a patient in
the beach-chair position is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3 Intraoperative photograph shows a patient in the beach-chair position.
(Courtesy of Donald J. Scholten II, MD, PhD, Winston-Salem, NC, and Brian R. Waterman,
MD, Winston-Salem, NC.)
A combination of regional neuraxial and general anesthesia may be used. General
anesthesia allows for beach-chair or lateral decubitus patient positioning. If conversion
to an open approach may be necessary, then general anesthesia is required. General

anesthesia allows for the implementation of hypotensive anesthesia to improve
visualization while limiting the need for pump or hydrostatic pressure with elevation of
arthroscopic irrigation.15,16 Regional anesthesia may allow for improved postoperative
pain control and may facilitate timely discharge from the postanesthesia care unit.17
Instruments and Implants
Depending on the procedure to be performed, minor adjustments in instruments and
implants may be required. General necessary instruments include:1
A standard 4.0-mm 30° arthroscope (some procedures may require a 70° arthroscope for
adequate visualization)
Camera/monitor and inflow/outflow pump and suction with appropriate arthroscopy tower
Spinal needle (18 gauge) for portal establishment
Cannulas of varying sizes to aid in maintenance of portals and fluid management
Graspers, biters, blunt arthroscopic probe
Arthroscopic scissors, arthroscopic suture cutters, antegrade/retrograde suture passing
devices
Wissinger rod/switching stick for transitioning cannulas between portals
Arthroscopic shaver, hooded burr for débridement and decompression
90-degree radiofrequency wand for hemostasis and tissue ablation
Relevant Shoulder Surface Anatomy

Relevant Shoulder Surface Anatomy
Important anatomic landmarks for shoulder arthroscopy include the acromion, coracoid,
clavicle, proximal humerus, and acromioclavicular joint1,3,18,19
Knowledge of the underlying anatomy of the glenohumeral joint is essential for
recognizing surface anatomic landmarks to establish arthroscopic portals. Relevant
surface anatomy may help guide portal placement and safe shoulder arthroscopy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000046
6/16

Important osseous structures include the acromion, clavicle, coracoid process, proximal
humerus, and acromioclavicular joint. The anterior, lateral, and posterior borders of the
acromion should be marked. A triangle can be constructed using the anterolateral
border of the acromion, the posterolateral border of the acromion, and the soft spot
more medially between the acromion and the clavicle. Tracing posteriorly from the
posterolateral border of the acromion, the scapular spine is identified. Anteriorly, the
coracoid process can be palpated just anterior to the distal third of the clavicle. The
acromioclavicular joint can be identified as a depression that exits directly anterior to the
soft spot identified between the clavicle and acromion.
Approach/Portal Placement
The posterior portal usually is established first as the primary viewing portal.
The anteroinferior (rotator interval) portal is established under direct visualization from the
posterior portal via the outside-in technique with the use of a spinal needle.
The anterolateral portal is most useful for viewing or as a working portal during subacromial
decompression, distal clavicle excision, and rotator cuff repair.
The Neviaser portal may aid in suture passage during superior labrum anterior to posterior
repair and for suprascapular nerve decompression.
The 5-o’clock portal aids in surgery along the anterior and inferior glenoid neck, including
Bankart repair.
The 7-o'clock portal may aid in loose body removal or posterior labrum fixation.

Approach/Portal Placement
Posterior portal: This is the first portal established and will serve as the primary viewing
portal. It is located in the posterior soft spot between the humeral head and the glenoid,
typically 2 to 3 cm medial and 1 to 2 cm inferior to the posterolateral corner of the
acromion. Gentle internal and external rotation of the humerus may help define the
location of the interval between the humeral head and the glenoid. Optional insufflation
of the joint with fluid may help distend the joint. A blunt trocar is inserted, aiming for the
coracoid process through the posterior capsule of the glenohumeral joint.1-3 (Video 2)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000046
7/16

Anteroinferior (rotator interval) portal: Establishment of the anterior portal is performed
under direct visualization from the posterior portal via outside-in technique with a spinal
needle. The topographic location is approximately 1 to 2 cm inferomedial to the
anterolateral corner of the acromion, paying close attention to remain lateral to the
coracoid process. When viewing from inside the glenohumeral joint, the ideal position is
within the rotator interval with the exact location varying depending on the pathology
being managed. A spinal needle is inserted to confirm correct positioning before making
a skin incision and inserting the blunt trocar.
Anterolateral portal: This portal is most useful for viewing or as a working portal during
subacromial decompression, distal clavicle excision, and rotator cuff repair. The location
typically is 1 to 3 cm distal to the lateral edge of the acromion just posterior to the
anterolateral edge of the acromion. This location can be confirmed via a spinal needle to
ensure the proposed portal location will provide an adequate trajectory for subsequent
tasks. A portal that is too proximal may hinder proper use because of the acromion; a
portal that is too distal (5 cm from acromion) endangers the axillary nerve.
Neviaser portal: This portal may aid in suture passage during superior labrum anterior
posterior repair and for suprascapular nerve decompression. It is created in the soft
spot between the posterior distal clavicle, the medial acromion, and the anterior
scapular spine.
Anteroinferior (5-o’clock) portal:20 This portal is helpful for surgery along the anterior
and inferior glenoid neck, including Bankart repair. This portal is created via inside-out
technique, with a switching stick aimed through the subscapularis and lateral to the
coracoid tip. It is important to remain within 2 cm of the proximal margin of the
subscapularis to avoid neurovascular injury.
Posteroinferior (7-o’clock) portal:21 This portal may aid in loose body removal or
posterior labrum fixation. This portal is created via inside-out technique, with a switching
stick from the anterior portal aimed past the 7-o’clock position on the glenoid and
pushed out through the posterior capsule. It typically is located 5 cm distal to the
posterolateral corner of the acromion. Figure 4 demonstrates surface anatomy and
possible locations for portals used in arthroscopy.3

Diagnostic Arthroscopy Evaluation

Diagnostic Anthroscopy Evaluation
Use a systematic approach for diagnostic shoulder arthroscopy (Table 1) to ensure
thorough and complete assessment of shoulder pathology.2,22,23

For evaluation of trainees, a grading system, such as the Arthroscopic Surgical Skill
Evaluation Tool, is recommended24 (Resource 4). This system evaluates overarching
principles vital to the execution of successful arthroscopy. A checklist of tasks to be
accomplished is supplied in Table 1.25
Table 1 Checklist of tasks to be accomplished during diagnostic shoulder arthroscopy

bicipital groove into the joint.

5

6

7

8

9

12


Diagnostic Arthroscopy Evaluation
With the arthroscope placed in the posterior portal, examine the superior glenoid
surface, the superior labrum, and the biceps tendon and anchor. Inspect the superior
labrum and the biceps tendon for signs of inflammation, fraying, or tears. A probe can
be inserted from the anterior portal to assist in interrogation of these and other
structures.
Rotate the arthroscope superiorly, and examine the course of the biceps tendon, taking
note of the superior glenohumeral ligament. Externally rotating the humerus may aid in
visualization of the biceps tendon course. Rotate the arthroscope to assess the middle
glenohumeral ligament and the subscapularis tendon. Note any anatomic variation in
the middle glenohumeral ligament and labrum, such as a Buford complex.26 Internal
and external rotation of the humerus may enhance assessment of the integrity of the
subscapularis tendon.
Advance the arthroscope to the anterior-inferior glenoid to inspect the labrum for
Bankart lesions, which are responsible for anterior shoulder instability. Rotate the
arthroscope inferiorly to assess the axillary pouch and the posterior recess for loose
bodies and to evaluate the posterior capsular attachments. Rotate and retract the
arthroscope slightly to visualize the posterior glenoid and labrum. Rotate and swing the
arthroscope superiorly to inspect the attachments of the supraspinatus and
infraspinatus tendons to the greater tuberosity of the proximal humerus. Inspect the
posterior humeral head for potential Hill-Sachs lesions in the setting of anterior
instability.
Enter the subacromial space through the posterior portal. Rotate the arthroscope
superiorly to inspect the undersurface of the acromion, the acromioclavicular joint, and
